Fit a distributional regression model

Source: R/fit.R
regcomp.Rd

Every regression parameter of the response distribution gets its own linear predictor on its link scale. The first formula gives the response and the predictor of the main parameter: the parameter equal to the mean if there is one, else the location, scale or rate parameter, else the first regression parameter (for example scale of the Weibull law, so that survival models are accelerated failure time models); further formulas such as sigma ~ x or shape ~ x give predictors for other parameters, which otherwise are constant. Predictors may contain offsets, factors and interactions, random effects in lme4 syntax ((1 | g), (1 + x | g), uncorrelated (1 + x || g), nested (1 | a/b), crossed (1 | a) + (1 | b)), structured random effects for longitudinal and spatial data written as glmmTMB style wrappers, and smooth terms s() and t2() from 'mgcv', which are fitted in their mixed model representation (as in mgcv::gamm()). Tensor products te() and ti() have no such representation; use t2() instead.

Usage

regcomp(
  formula,
  ...,
  family,
  data,
  engine = c("ml", "tmb", "bayes"),
  weights = NULL,
  links = NULL,
  fixed = NULL,
  penalty = NULL,
  priors = NULL,
  control = regcomp_control(),
  parameterization = NULL,
  subset = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

Two sided formula response ~ predictors for the first regression parameter. The response may be wrapped in cens() or surv().

...

Further formulas for other parameters, such as sigma ~ x, and data arguments of the family (for example trials = n for the binomial), evaluated in data.

family

A family identifier, family object or a family built by an operator such as inflate().

data

A data frame.

engine

"ml", "tmb" or "bayes".

weights

Optional prior weights multiplying each log likelihood contribution.

links

Optional named list or character vector of link names per parameter.

fixed

Optional named list of parameters held fixed at given values (not estimated).

penalty

Optional penalty from penalty() (engine "ml").

priors

Optional priors from prior() (engine "bayes").

control

List of control settings, see regcomp_control().

parameterization

Optional parameterization name passed to get_family().

subset

Optional logical or index vector selecting rows of data.

Value

An object of class regcomp_fit.

Random effect structures

A bar term may be wrapped in a covariance structure:

  • us(x | g): unstructured (the default for |); diag(x | g) and homdiag(x | g): independent effects with separate or common variance (the default for ||).

  • cs(0 + time | g) and homcs(0 + time | g): compound symmetry with heterogeneous or common variances.

  • ar1(0 + time | g): first order autoregressive correlation rho^|i - j| across the columns (time must be a factor with equally spaced, ordered levels), with a common variance.

  • ou(t | g) or exp(t | g): continuous time autoregressive (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) correlation exp(-|t_i - t_j| / range) for unequally spaced numeric times; gau(x + y | g) and matern32(x + y | g) give Gaussian and Matern (smoothness 3/2) correlation in the coordinates on the left of the bar, for spatial effects. One random effect is created per distinct coordinate.

Structured random effects are available in every parameter and for every family, so a latent autoregressive process can enter a count, survival or ordinal model. The Bayesian engine supports us and diag structures.

Engines

  • "ml": maximum likelihood in R. Without random effects or smooths the log likelihood is maximized by nlminb() with an analytic chain rule gradient. With random effects or smooths the marginal likelihood is approximated by the Laplace method (joint over all random effects, so crossed and nested factors and random effects in several parameters are allowed); the fitted object records approximation = "laplace". Penalties (see penalty()) give penalized likelihood estimates.

  • "tmb": the same model, random effects and covariance structures through automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation of 'TMB' (via 'RTMB'), for the normal, Poisson, binomial, Bernoulli, NB1, NB2, Student t, gamma, lognormal, Weibull, beta and exponential families (see family_capabilities()). It gives the same estimates as "ml" and is much faster for large multilevel models; the taped density is checked against the registry density before fitting.

  • "bayes": Bayesian inference. A 'Stan' program is generated from the same specification (see stan_code()) and run by 'bayescompR' (default, no compiler needed), 'cmdstanr' or 'rstan'. Priors are set with prior().

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(300), z = rnorm(300))
d$y <- rnbinom(300, mu = exp(1 + 0.5 * d$x), size = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$z))
fit <- regcomp(y ~ x, phi ~ z, family = "nb2", data = d)
summary(fit)
#> <regcomp_fit> Negative binomial (NB2) regression, engine 'ml' (frequentist)
#>   mu (log link): ~x
#>   phi (log link): ~z
#>   log likelihood -637.197 on 4 parameters, n = 300
#> 
#> Wald estimates with 95% confidence intervals:
#>                 estimate std_error  lower  upper       z p_value
#> mu:(Intercept)    0.9818    0.0547 0.8745 1.0890 17.9431  0.0000
#> mu:x              0.6232    0.0593 0.5070 0.7395 10.5090  0.0000
#> phi:(Intercept)   0.7865    0.1651 0.4628 1.1101  4.7631  0.0000
#> phi:z             0.4709    0.1645 0.1486 0.7933  2.8635  0.0042
#> max |gradient| 2.84e-05; Hessian positive definite 
head(predict(fit, type = "mean"))
#>        1        2        3        4        5        6 
#> 1.806405 2.992792 1.585622 7.213584 3.277602 1.600675 
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 0, z = 0), type = "quantile",
        probs = c(0.1, 0.9))
#> [1] 0 6
